key_facts: In 1968, 3M scientist Spencer Silver invented a low-tack, reusable adhesive while trying to create a super strong glue.
The adhesive remained unused at 3M for five years.
In 1974, coworker Art Fry used the adhesive to keep bookmarks from falling out of his choir songbook.
After initial commercial failure in 1977, free sample distributions in Boise, Idaho in 1978 won consumers over.
Post-it notes officially launched across the United States in 1980.
The iconic yellow color was selected purely by chance because the adjacent laboratory only had yellow scrap paper available.
package.script: You've stuck a Post-it note, but why did its glue sit unused for five years before a singer saved it? Here's how a failed glue became the sticky note. He tried the weak glue, and the bookmark stayed put, then peeled off clean. After a flop in nineteen seventy-seven, free samples in Boise, Idaho won people over. They went on sale across America in nineteen eighty, yellow because that was the scrap paper next door. So the glue waited five years because it was a solution without a problem, until a bookmark. What's the weirdest place you've stuck a sticky note? And next time you peel one off, remember...

package.script:
How does a thermos keep coffee hot
for twelve whole hours?
Heat escapes in three ways.
It can touch its way out,
that's conduction.
It can ride on moving air,
that's convection.
Or it can glow away as invisible light,
called radiation.
A thermos blocks all three.
It's really two bottles,
one inside the other,
and the gap between them is a vacuum.
With no air in there,
heat has nothing to touch,
and nothing to ride.
Then the walls are shiny,
like a mirror,
so the glow bounces back into your coffee.
A scientist named James Dewar
invented it in 1892,
to keep liquid gases ice cold.
The only real leak?
The lid.
So what's the longest your coffee ever stayed hot?
key_facts: Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation
A vacuum flask is two walls with a vacuum between them, which blocks conduction and convection
Silvered/shiny walls reflect infrared radiation back
Invented by Scottish scientist James Dewar in 1892 to store liquefied gases
Most remaining heat loss is through the stopper/lid
Good flasks keep drinks hot for around 12 hours

package.title: How a Plane Toilet Flushes at 35,000 Feet ✈️
package.description:
How does an airplane toilet flush? Plane toilets are vacuum toilets: a valve opens the bowl to the thin air outside, the higher cabin pressure shoves everything into a tank at the back, and below 16,000 feet an electric vacuum pump does the job instead.

package.pinned_comment: Have you ever jumped when a plane toilet flushed? Be honest 😂
package.script:
How does a plane toilet flush
at thirty-five thousand feet?
It barely uses water.
It uses the sky.
Your cabin is pressurized,
packed with air like a balloon.
Outside, the air is super thin.
Press the button,
and a valve opens a pipe
from the bowl to that thin outside air.
The high pressure in the cabin
shoves everything down the pipe.
That's the whoosh.
It all lands in a tank at the back of the plane.
About three seconds later,
the valve slams shut.
But below sixteen thousand feet,
the outside air isn't thin enough,
so an electric pump makes the vacuum instead.
And no, nothing gets dumped in the sky.
Ground crews empty the tank after landing.
So, next flight,
are you brave enough to press it?
key_facts: Airplane toilets are vacuum toilets (patented by James Kemper in 1975, on Boeing jets by 1982)
At altitude a valve connects the bowl to low outside pressure; higher cabin pressure pushes waste through
Waste goes to a tank at the rear of the aircraft
Valves close after about 3-4 seconds
Below about 16,000 ft (and on the ground) an electric vacuum generator creates the suction
Waste is not dumped in flight; ground service trucks empty the tank after landing

package.script:
What actually happens to your food,
after you swallow it?
It's one of the longest trips in your body.
And for most of history,
nobody really knew how it worked.
Many ancient doctors thought the stomach
simply cooked your food, like a pot.
Then, in the seventeen hundreds,
scientists fed animals
food sealed inside little metal tubes.
The food couldn't be squished,
but it still dissolved.
Italian scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani
even tried it on himself,
swallowing tiny linen bags of food.
The answer was a liquid.
He called it gastric juice.
So let's follow one bite,
all the way through.
Step one: your mouth.
Your teeth crush the bite into mush,
and saliva soaks it.
Saliva holds an enzyme called amylase,
that starts turning starch into sugar,
before you even swallow.
Then your tongue pushes the food back,
and a tiny flap, the epiglottis,
folds down over your windpipe,
so nothing goes the wrong way.
Now the food enters the esophagus,
a muscle tube about twenty-five centimeters long.
It doesn't just fall.
Rings of muscle squeeze behind it,
like toothpaste in a tube.
That's called peristalsis.
The trip takes about nine seconds,
and it works even upside down.
Next stop, the stomach.
It's a stretchy bag of muscle,
filled with hydrochloric acid.
Stomach acid can drop to around pH two,
about as sour as lemon juice.
It kills a lot of germs,
and helps an enzyme called pepsin
start chopping up protein.
About three times a minute,
the stomach walls squeeze and churn,
mixing everything into a thick soup called chyme.
That can take two to four hours.
So why doesn't your stomach digest itself?
Its lining makes a thick coat of mucus,
plus bicarbonate to calm the acid.
And the lining cells get replaced every few days.
Then a little valve opens,
and lets the chyme out, a squirt at a time,
into the small intestine.
This is where the real magic happens.
It's about five meters long,
coiled up inside your belly.
Your liver sends in bile,
which breaks fat into tiny droplets.
Your pancreas adds more enzymes,
and neutralizes the acid.
The walls are covered in millions of tiny fingers,
called villi,
and those are covered in even tinier microvilli.
Spread flat, scientists estimate your gut lining
covers about thirty-two square meters.
That's half a badminton court!
Old textbooks said a whole tennis court,
but half a court is still huge.
Right here, most of the nutrients
slip into your blood.
What's left moves on to the large intestine.
It's wider, but only about one and a half meters long.
Its main job is soaking up water.
And it's home to trillions of bacteria.
Scientists estimate about thirty-eight trillion live in you,
mostly right here.
They munch the fiber you can't digest,
and make some vitamins in return.
So how long does the whole trip take?
About six hours through the stomach and small intestine,
and up to another two days in the large intestine.
Whatever your body can't use,
leaves at the end.
But the rest?
That bite became your energy,
your muscles,
even the thoughts you're having right now.
So which food do you think
takes the longest trip?
key_facts: Ancient physicians described digestion as 'concoction', a kind of cooking in the stomach; in the 1750s Réaumur fed a bird food in perforated metal tubes and the food still dissolved (Popular Science Monthly, 1909)
Lazzaro Spallanzani experimented on animals and himself in the 1770s-80s and named the stomach's solvent 'gastric juice' (whonamedit; Popular Science Monthly)
Saliva's amylase starts breaking starch into sugar; the epiglottis covers the windpipe during swallowing
The esophagus is about 25 cm; peristalsis carries food to the stomach in roughly 9 seconds and works upside down (Straight Dope / standard physiology)
Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid, around pH 1.5-3.5; mucus and bicarbonate from foveolar cells protect the lining (Wikipedia: Foveolar cell)
Small intestine about 3-5 m in living adults; bile emulsifies fat, pancreatic juice neutralises acid; villi and microvilli; most nutrient absorption happens here (Wikipedia: Small intestine)
Gut lining surface ~32 m2, about half a badminton court, not a tennis court (Helander & Fändriks 2014, via PopSci)
About 6 hours through stomach and small intestine; up to 36-48 hours in the colon (Mayo Clinic)
About 38 trillion bacteria in the body, mostly in the colon (Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016)

package.script:
How did people in old Japan
smell what time it was?
No gears. No ticking.
Just a box of ash.
First, they smoothed white ash flat,
and pressed a stamp into it.
That left a groove,
a maze that snakes back and forth.
They filled the groove with incense powder:
one long, thin trail.
Light one end,
and a tiny ember crawls through the maze,
at a nearly steady speed.
Here's the clever part.
At set marks along the trail,
they switched to a different incense.
So when the smell in the room changed,
you knew more time had passed.
Some trails burned for twelve hours.
Some lasted a whole month.
A few even dropped a little ball
onto a tray, like an alarm.
So, what time does your room smell like right now?
key_facts: Seal-type incense clocks (Japanese ko-dokei) laid a continuous trail of incense powder in a pattern pressed into flattened ash with a stamp or stencil
The powder burned at a fairly steady rate, so elapsed time could be read from how far the ember had travelled
Markers or tablets of different incense placed along the trail changed the aroma when reached, so an attendant could tell the time by smell
Burn times ranged from about 12 hours to a month, depending on trail length
Some versions dropped balls into a tray when the incense burned through, as an audible signal
Incense clocks came to Japan from China and were used in Japan from the Nara period

package.script:
How does a plane toilet flush
at thirty-five thousand feet?
It barely uses water.
It uses the sky.
Your cabin is pressurized,
packed with air like a balloon.
Outside, the air is super thin.
Press the button,
and a valve opens a pipe
from the bowl to that thin outside air.
The high pressure in the cabin
shoves everything down the pipe.
That's the whoosh.
It all lands in a tank at the back of the plane.
About three seconds later,
the valve slams shut.
But below sixteen thousand feet,
the outside air isn't thin enough,
so an electric pump makes the vacuum instead.
And no, nothing gets dumped in the sky.
Ground crews empty the tank after landing.
So, next flight,
are you brave enough to press it?
key_facts: Airplane toilets are vacuum toilets (patented by James Kemper in 1975, on Boeing jets by 1982)
At altitude a valve connects the bowl to low outside pressure; higher cabin pressure pushes waste through
Waste goes to a tank at the rear of the aircraft
Valves close after about 3-4 seconds
Below about 16,000 ft (and on the ground) an electric vacuum generator creates the suction
Waste is not dumped in flight; ground service trucks empty the tank after landing

package.script:
What actually happens to your food,
after you swallow it?
It's one of the longest trips in your body.
And for most of history,
nobody really knew how it worked.
Many ancient doctors thought the stomach
simply cooked your food, like a pot.
Then, in the seventeen hundreds,
scientists fed animals
food sealed inside little metal tubes.
The food couldn't be squished,
but it still dissolved.
Italian scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani
even tried it on himself,
swallowing tiny linen bags of food.
The answer was a liquid.
He called it gastric juice.
So let's follow one bite,
all the way through.
Step one: your mouth.
Your teeth crush the bite into mush,
and saliva soaks it.
Saliva holds an enzyme called amylase,
that starts turning starch into sugar,
before you even swallow.
Then your tongue pushes the food back,
and a tiny flap, the epiglottis,
folds down over your windpipe,
so nothing goes the wrong way.
Now the food enters the esophagus,
a muscle tube about twenty-five centimeters long.
It doesn't just fall.
Rings of muscle squeeze behind it,
like toothpaste in a tube.
That's called peristalsis.
The trip takes about nine seconds,
and it works even upside down.
Next stop, the stomach.
It's a stretchy bag of muscle,
filled with hydrochloric acid.
Stomach acid can drop to around pH two,
about as sour as lemon juice.
It kills a lot of germs,
and helps an enzyme called pepsin
start chopping up protein.
About three times a minute,
the stomach walls squeeze and churn,
mixing everything into a thick soup called chyme.
That can take two to four hours.
So why doesn't your stomach digest itself?
Its lining makes a thick coat of mucus,
plus bicarbonate to calm the acid.
And the lining cells get replaced every few days.
Then a little valve opens,
and lets the chyme out, a squirt at a time,
into the small intestine.
This is where the real magic happens.
It's about five meters long,
coiled up inside your belly.
Your liver sends in bile,
which breaks fat into tiny droplets.
Your pancreas adds more enzymes,
and neutralizes the acid.
The walls are covered in millions of tiny fingers,
called villi,
and those are covered in even tinier microvilli.
Spread flat, scientists estimate your gut lining
covers about thirty-two square meters.
That's half a badminton court!
Old textbooks said a whole tennis court,
but half a court is still huge.
Right here, most of the nutrients
slip into your blood.
What's left moves on to the large intestine.
It's wider, but only about one and a half meters long.
Its main job is soaking up water.
And it's home to trillions of bacteria.
Scientists estimate about thirty-eight trillion live in you,
mostly right here.
They munch the fiber you can't digest,
and make some vitamins in return.
So how long does the whole trip take?
About six hours through the stomach and small intestine,
and up to another two days in the large intestine.
Whatever your body can't use,
leaves at the end.
But the rest?
That bite became your energy,
your muscles,
even the thoughts you're having right now.
So which food do you think
takes the longest trip?

Lazzaro Spallanzani experimented on animals and himself in the 1770s-80s and named the stomach's solvent 'gastric juice' (whonamedit; Popular Science Monthly)
Saliva's amylase starts breaking starch into sugar; the epiglottis covers the windpipe during swallowing
The esophagus is about 25 cm; peristalsis carries food to the stomach in roughly 9 seconds and works upside down (Straight Dope / standard physiology)
Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid, around pH 1.5-3.5; mucus and bicarbonate from foveolar cells protect the lining (Wikipedia: Foveolar cell)
Small intestine about 3-5 m in living adults; bile emulsifies fat, pancreatic juice neutralises acid; villi and microvilli; most nutrient absorption happens here (Wikipedia: Small intestine)
Gut lining surface ~32 m2, about half a badminton court, not a tennis court (Helander & Fändriks 2014, via PopSci)
About 6 hours through stomach and small intestine; up to 36-48 hours in the colon (Mayo Clinic)
About 38 trillion bacteria in the body, mostly in the colon (Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016)

Italian scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani

14
00:00:29,400 --> 00:00:31,010
even tried it on himself,

15
00:00:31,310 --> 00:00:33,560
swallowing tiny linen bags of food.

16
00:00:34,110 --> 00:00:35,620
The answer was a liquid.

17
00:00:36,170 --> 00:00:37,840
He called it gastric juice.

18
00:00:38,390 --> 00:00:39,880
So let's follow one bite,

19
00:00:40,180 --> 00:00:41,260
all the way through.

20
00:00:41,810 --> 00:00:43,120
Step one: your mouth.

21
00:00:43,670 --> 00:00:45,570
Your teeth crush the bite into mush,

22
00:00:45,870 --> 00:00:47,120
and saliva soaks it.

23
00:00:47,670 --> 00:00:50,190
Saliva holds an enzyme called amylase,

24
00:00:50,490 --> 00:00:52,520
that starts turning starch into sugar,

25
00:00:52,820 --> 00:00:54,190
before you even swallow.

26
00:00:54,740 --> 00:00:56,710
Then your tongue pushes the food back,

27
00:00:57,010 --> 00:00:59,030
and a tiny flap, the epiglottis,

28
00:00:59,330 --> 00:01:01,220
folds down over your windpipe,

29
00:01:01,520 --> 00:01:03,270
so nothing goes the wrong way.

30
00:01:03,820 --> 00:01:05,930
Now the food enters the esophagus,

31
00:01:06,230 --> 00:01:09,190
a muscle tube about twenty-five centimeters long.

32
00:01:09,740 --> 00:01:10,950
It doesn't just fall.

33
00:01:11,500 --> 00:01:13,480
Rings of muscle squeeze behind it,

34
00:01:13,780 --> 00:01:15,360
like toothpaste in a tube.

35
00:01:15,910 --> 00:01:17,420
That's called peristalsis.

36
00:01:17,970 --> 00:01:19,940
The trip takes about nine seconds,

37
00:01:20,240 --> 00:01:22,050
and it works even upside down.

38
00:01:22,600 --> 00:01:23,920
Next stop, the stomach.

39
00:01:24,470 --> 00:01:26,110
It's a stretchy bag of muscle,

40
00:01:26,410 --> 00:01:28,230
filled with hydrochloric acid.

41
00:01:28,780 --> 00:01:31,430
Stomach acid can drop to around pH two,

42
00:01:31,730 --> 00:01:33,620
about as sour as lemon juice.

43
00:01:34,170 --> 00:01:35,820
It kills a lot of germs,

44
00:01:36,120 --> 00:01:38,000
and helps an enzyme called pepsin

45
00:01:38,300 --> 00:01:39,840
start chopping up protein.

46
00:01:40,390 --> 00:01:41,890
About three times a minute,

47
00:01:42,190 --> 00:01:44,190
the stomach walls squeeze and churn,

48
00:01:44,490 --> 00:01:47,180
mixing everything into a thick soup called chyme.

49
00:01:47,730 --> 00:01:49,620
That can take two to four hours.

50
00:01:50,170 --> 00:01:52,650
So why doesn't your stomach digest itself?

51
00:01:53,200 --> 00:01:55,460
Its lining makes a thick coat of mucus,

52
00:01:55,760 --> 00:01:57,970
plus bicarbonate to calm the acid.

53
00:01:58,520 --> 00:02:01,560
And the lining cells get replaced every few days.

54
00:02:02,110 --> 00:02:03,710
Then a little valve opens,

55
00:02:04,010 --> 00:02:06,500
and lets the chyme out, a squirt at a time,

56
00:02:06,800 --> 00:02:08,320
into the small intestine.

57
00:02:08,870 --> 00:02:11,160
This is where the real magic happens.

58
00:02:11,710 --> 00:02:13,330
It's about five meters long,

59
00:02:13,630 --> 00:02:15,260
coiled up inside your belly.

60
00:02:15,810 --> 00:02:17,240
Your liver sends in bile,

61
00:02:17,540 --> 00:02:19,800
which breaks fat into tiny droplets.

62
00:02:20,350 --> 00:02:22,340
Your pancreas adds more enzymes,

63
00:02:22,640 --> 00:02:24,340
and neutralizes the acid.

64
00:02:24,890 --> 00:02:28,110
The walls are covered in millions of tiny fingers,

65
00:02:28,410 --> 00:02:29,320
called villi,

66
00:02:29,620 --> 00:02:32,770
and those are covered in even tinier microvilli.

67
00:02:33,320 --> 00:02:36,300
Spread flat, scientists estimate your gut lining

68
00:02:36,600 --> 00:02:38,850
covers about thirty-two square meters.

69
00:02:39,400 --> 00:02:41,050
That's half a badminton court!

70
00:02:41,600 --> 00:02:43,690
Old textbooks said a whole tennis court,

71
00:02:43,990 --> 00:02:45,760
but half a court is still huge.

72
00:02:46,310 --> 00:02:48,210
Right here, most of the nutrients

73
00:02:48,510 --> 00:02:49,780
slip into your blood.

74
00:02:50,330 --> 00:02:52,850
What's left moves on to the large intestine.

75
00:02:53,400 --> 00:02:56,570
It's wider, but only about one and a half meters long.

76
00:02:57,120 --> 00:02:59,180
Its main job is soaking up water.

77
00:02:59,730 --> 00:03:01,950
And it's home to trillions of bacteria.

78
00:03:02,500 --> 00:03:05,700
Scientists estimate about thirty-eight trillion live in you,

79
00:03:06,000 --> 00:03:07,230
mostly right here.

80
00:03:07,780 --> 00:03:09,880
They munch the fiber you can't digest,

81
00:03:10,180 --> 00:03:12,050
and make some vitamins in return.

82
00:03:12,600 --> 00:03:14,620
So how long does the whole trip take?

83
00:03:15,170 --> 00:03:18,200
About six hours through the stomach and small intestine,

84
00:03:18,500 --> 00:03:21,550
and up to another two days in the large intestine.

85
00:03:22,100 --> 00:03:23,890
Whatever your body can't use,

86
00:03:24,190 --> 00:03:25,250
leaves at the end.

87
00:03:25,800 --> 00:03:26,660
But the rest?

88
00:03:27,210 --> 00:03:28,950
That bite became your energy,

89
00:03:29,250 --> 00:03:30,140
your muscles,

90
00:03:30,440 --> 00:03:32,510
even the thoughts you're having right now.

91
00:03:33,060 --> 00:03:34,430
So which food do you think

92
00:03:34,730 --> 00:03:36,100
takes the longest trip?

topic.title: Why do bats sleep upside down?

package.description:
Why do bats sleep upside down? Bats can't take off from the ground like birds, so they hang high up by their toes, let go and drop straight into flight, while a tendon lock in their feet keeps them hanging with zero muscle effort.

package.pinned_comment: Could you nap upside down like a bat? How long do you think you'd last? 🦇
package.script:
You'd pass out sleeping upside down,
but some bats do it 20 hours a day.
So why hang like that?
Bats have a takeoff problem.
They're the only mammals that truly fly,
but their wings can't lift them off the ground,
and their back legs are too tiny to run.
So they sleep up high, hanging by their toes.
Time to go?
They let go, drop,
and they're flying before they hit anything.
But doesn't hanging all day get tiring?
Nope.
Their toe tendons work like a locking clip.
Body weight pulls the tendon tight,
and the claws clamp shut, with zero effort.
To let go, they use muscles to open them.
And the blood rush to the head?
Bats are so light, it barely happens.
Plus, up high, most predators can't reach them.
So, could you nap upside down like a bat?
key_facts: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight
Bat wings can't generate enough lift from a standstill on the ground, and their hind legs are too small and light to run for a takeoff
Hanging lets them simply let go and drop into flight
Tendons in the feet are pulled tight by the bat's body weight, closing the claws with no muscle effort; muscles are needed to open them
Bats are light enough that blood pooling in the head is not a problem
Roosting high keeps them out of reach of most predators
Some species like the little brown bat sleep around 19-20 hours a day

topic.title: How do smoke detectors know there's a fire?

package.title: How Smoke Alarms Smell Smoke ☢️
package.description:
How does a smoke detector know there's a fire? Ionization smoke alarms use a speck of radioactive americium-241 to make the air carry a tiny current that smoke interrupts, while photoelectric alarms catch light scattered by smoke onto a hidden sensor.

package.pinned_comment: Check the label on yours: does it say ionization (radioactive) or photoelectric (light)? Tell me which one you've got 👇
package.script:
Your smoke alarm might be radioactive.
Nobody tells you,
but that's how it smells smoke.
Inside sits a speck of americium,
which fires out tiny alpha particles.
They slam into the air
between two metal plates,
knocking electrons loose.
Now the air carries electricity,
so a tiny, steady current flows.
When smoke drifts in,
bits of smoke grab those charged particles.
The current drops,
and the alarm screams.
Other alarms use light instead.
An LED shines across a dark chamber,
away from a sensor.
No smoke, no light hits it.
But smoke scatters the beam,
bouncing light into the sensor.
Beep!
And that americium?
Its half-life is four hundred thirty-two years,
so it outlasts your alarm by centuries.
So, is the one above your bed
radioactive, or running on light?
key_facts: Ionization smoke alarms contain a small amount of americium-241, which emits alpha particles
Alpha particles ionize air between two electrodes, sustaining a small steady current
Smoke entering the chamber disrupts/reduces the current; below a threshold the alarm sounds
Photoelectric alarms shine an LED across a chamber away from a photocell; smoke scatters light onto the sensor
Americium-241 half-life is about 432 years (EPA: 432.2)
Smoke alarms are typically replaced about every 10 years

package.description:
How does electricity get from the power plant to your outlet? package.pinned_comment: Before this video, did you think the electrons themselves raced from the power plant to your outlet? ⚡
package.script: Up to seven hundred sixty-five thousand volts flow through the biggest power lines, yet your outlet gives you just a hundred twenty. Here's how. It all starts with a spinning magnet, maybe hundreds of miles away. So let's follow the trip, in simple words. Stop one: the power plant. Almost every power plant does the same job. It spins something. Coal, gas and nuclear plants boil water into steam. Dams use falling water. Wind farms use, well, wind. All of it pushes the blades of a turbine, and the turbine spins a giant magnet inside coils of copper wire. Here's the trick, found by Michael Faraday back in 1831. When a magnet moves past a wire, it shoves the electrons inside that wire. Spin it nonstop, and you get a nonstop push. That push is electricity. And because the magnet keeps flipping north and south, the push swings back and forth too. In the US, it swings sixty times every second. In most of the world, it's fifty. That's called alternating current. Stop two: the voltage jump. A generator makes about twenty thousand volts. But right outside the plant, a step-up transformer cranks it way higher, up to seven hundred sixty-five thousand volts on the biggest lines. Why make it so extreme? Think of a garden hose. You can move a lot of water slowly through a fat hose, or the same water super fast through a thin one. Power lines work the same way. Crank the voltage up, and the current, the flow, drops way down. Less current means less heat wasted in the wires. Even so, about five percent of the power is lost as heat along the way. Stop three: the step back down. Seven hundred thousand volts would fry your toaster instantly. So the lines run into a substation, where big transformers drop it to a few thousand volts. Those smaller lines run down your street. Then one last transformer, that gray can on the pole, or a green box on the lawn, brings it down to what your house uses: a hundred twenty volts in the US, around two hundred thirty in much of the world. Stop four: your walls. The wire enters through a meter, which counts every bit you use, and then a breaker panel, which cuts the power if a wire gets too hot. From there, cables run to every outlet. And those holes aren't random. On a US outlet, the short slot is hot. That's where the push comes in. The tall slot is neutral, the path back. And the round hole is ground, a safety exit if something goes wrong. Now the wildest part. Flip a switch, and the light turns on instantly. But the electrons in the wire barely move. They crawl slower than a snail, mostly just wiggling back and forth. What races through the wire is the push itself, moving at close to the speed of light. So the energy in your charger left that spinning magnet a split second ago. Twenty thousand volts, then seven hundred sixty-five thousand, then down to the wall, all in the blink of an eye. Next time: if Earth is spinning so fast, why don't we fly off?
key_facts: Most power plants spin a turbine (steam from coal, gas or nuclear; falling water; wind) that turns a magnet inside copper coils; Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831
Grid power is alternating current: 60 Hz in the US, 50 Hz in most of the world
Generators put out roughly 20,000 volts (commonly cited 10,000-25,000); step-up transformers raise it to as much as 765,000 V on the biggest US lines
Higher voltage means lower current for the same power, so less is lost as heat; about 5% of US electricity is lost in transmission and distribution (EIA estimate)
Substations step down to a few thousand volts for distribution; pole-top or pad-mounted transformers bring it to 120/240 V in US homes (about 230 V in much of the world)
On a US outlet the shorter slot is hot, the taller slot is neutral and the round hole is ground
Electrons drift slowly (fractions of a millimetre per second) while the electrical signal/energy travels at a large fraction of the speed of light

Less current means less heat wasted in the wires.

00:01:47,590 --> 00:01:50,090

00:01:59,570 --> 00:02:01,750

00:02:08,940 --> 00:02:10,580

00:02:14,540 --> 00:02:16,820

00:02:17,120 --> 00:02:19,150

53
00:02:19,450 --> 00:02:22,260
around two hundred thirty in much of the world.

54
00:02:22,810 --> 00:02:24,340

55
00:02:24,890 --> 00:02:26,580
The wire enters through a meter,

56
00:02:26,880 --> 00:02:28,720

57
00:02:29,020 --> 00:02:30,320
and then a breaker panel,

58
00:02:30,620 --> 00:02:33,130
which cuts the power if a wire gets too hot.

59
00:02:33,680 --> 00:02:36,040
From there, cables run to every outlet.

60
00:02:36,590 --> 00:02:38,290
And those holes aren't random.

00:02:38,840 --> 00:02:41,520
On a US outlet, the short slot is hot.

00:02:42,070 --> 00:02:43,510
That's where the push comes in.

00:02:44,060 --> 00:02:45,640

the path back.

package.script:
A weed invented your Velcro,
in nineteen forty-one,
and almost nobody believed it.
A Swiss engineer, George de Mestral,
took his dog hiking in the Alps.
They came home covered in burrs,
the spiky seed heads of burdock.
Under a microscope,
every spike ended in a tiny hook,
and his clothes were full of tiny loops.
Hook meets loop,
and they grab on.
So he tried to copy it.
Cotton wore out too fast.
Nylon worked,
sewn under hot infrared light
into stiff little hooks.
It took him about ten years,
and the patent came in nineteen fifty-five.
He named it from two French words,
velours, for velvet,
and crochet, for hook.
Astronauts used it
to keep snack pouches from floating away.
So when your shoe straps rip open,
do you blame the weed, or the dog?

Under a microscope the burrs showed many tiny hooks that caught on loops in fabric and fur
Early cotton versions wore out quickly; nylon proved durable
Nylon hooks were formed by sewing nylon under hot infrared light
Development took about ten years; Swiss patent filed 1951, granted 1955
The name Velcro blends French velours (velvet) and crochet (hook)
NASA used Velcro on Apollo missions, including to hold food pouches in place in zero gravity

package.title: How Does a Pufferfish Puff Up? 🐡
package.description:
How does a pufferfish puff up? It gulps seawater into a folded, stretchy stomach that can expand up to 100 times, so its body balloons to about three times its size with spines sticking out.

package.pinned_comment: If you could puff up like a pufferfish, what would make you do it? 🐡
package.script: A pufferfish stomach stretches 100 times bigger, and you'd never guess why it has to. When a hungry fish gets close, the pufferfish opens its mouth wide and gulps seawater, fast. Gulp after gulp, it pumps the water into its stomach. That stomach is folded like an accordion, so it unfolds and keeps on stretching. There are almost no ribs in the way, so the whole body balloons out. Its stretchy skin pulls tight, and little spines pop up all over. Now it's about three times its size, a spiky ball way too big to swallow. But puffing up is hard work. It can take hours to catch its breath, so it only puffs when it has to. Then it spits the water back out. So if you were a pufferfish, what would make you puff?
key_facts: Pufferfish inflate by gulping water into their stomach, not air (in water)
The folded stomach can expand roughly 50-100 times (Texas Saltwater Fishing Magazine)
Puffers lack ribs (or most ribs) and a pelvis, so the body can become a ball
Stretchy collagen-rich skin goes taut; spines stand up
Inflated balloonfish reach about 3x normal volume (3-4x per Mental Floss)
Recovery: heavy breathing for up to about 5 hours afterward (Mental Floss)

topic.title: Why don't giraffes faint when they lift their heads?

package.title: A Giraffe's 11 kg Heart Stops It Fainting 🦒
package.description:
Why don't giraffes faint when they lift their heads? A giraffe's brain sits about two meters above its heart, so it relies on an 11 kg heart pumping at about twice our blood pressure, one-way valves in its neck veins, and super-tight leg skin that works like compression socks.

Sources:

https://stanfordbloodcenter.org/for-giraffes-blood-circulation-is-a-tall-order/

package.pinned_comment: If you had a giraffe's heart, do you think you'd ever get dizzy again? 🦒
package.script: You'd faint with your brain two meters up. Giraffes never do. Why? A giraffe swings its head from the water, all the way up to the treetops, and nothing happens. First, a monster heart. It weighs about eleven kilos, with walls thick enough to pump at twice your blood pressure. Second, valves in the neck veins. When the head drops down to drink, they stop blood flooding back into the brain. Third, scientists think the neck veins store blood, and when the head swings up, it rushes to the heart for one extra-strong beat. But all that pressure would make anyone's legs swell, so giraffes wear built-in compression socks: super-tight skin around their legs. So, if you had a giraffe's heart, would you still get dizzy with your brain two meters up?
key_facts: A giraffe's head sits about 2 m above its heart; head up to ~6 m above ground (Knowable Magazine)
Giraffe heart weighs about 25 lb / 11 kg (Stanford Blood Center)
Blood pressure at heart level ~220/180, roughly twice a human's (Knowable; Stanford)
Jugular vein valves stop backflow toward the brain when the head is lowered (Mitchell et al., Univ. of Pretoria)
Hypothesis: >1 L of blood pooled in neck veins returns to the heart when the head rises, giving a strong beat (Knowable, unconfirmed in awake giraffes)
Tight skin / dense connective tissue on the legs acts like support stockings (Knowable; Stanford)

topic.title: Why do your ears pop on a plane?

package.title: Why Your Ears Pop at 8,000 Feet ✈️
package.description:
Why do your ears pop on a plane? A plane cabin is only pressurized to about 6,000 to 8,000 feet, so the air trapped behind your eardrum pushes out on the climb and gets squeezed in on landing until your 3.5 cm Eustachian tube opens and evens out the pressure.

Sources:
https://acibademinternational.com/blog/why-do-your-ears-pop-pressure-altitude-and-the-tube-that-fixes-it/
https://www.scienceabc.com/eyeopeners/ears-pop-airplane-takes-off-landing-air-pressure-difference
https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/13104/why-do-our-ears-pop-when-we-ride-airplanes

tags: why do ears pop on a plane
package.pinned_comment: Be honest: on landing, are you a yawner or a swallower? ✈️
package.script: A three and a half centimeter tube in your skull is why your ears pop. It's called the Eustachian tube, and it links your middle ear to the back of your throat. Behind your eardrum sits a tiny pocket of air. On the ground, it matches the air outside. But a plane cabin is only pressurized like an eight thousand foot mountain. So as you climb, the outside pressure drops, and the air behind your eardrum pushes out. Your eardrum bulges like a balloon, until the tube cracks open, air puffs out, and pop! Landing is trickier. Now the cabin air squeezes in, and that pressure pinches the tube shut. So you swallow, or you yawn. Tiny muscles yank the tube open, air rushes in, and your eardrum snaps back flat. So next flight, will you open that secret tube with a yawn, or a swallow?
key_facts: Adult Eustachian tube is about 3.5 cm long, linking the middle ear to the back of the nose/throat (Acibadem)
Airliner cabins are pressurized to roughly the pressure at 6,000-8,000 ft (Acibadem)
On the climb, higher pressure in the middle ear pushes the tube open from inside; the pop is pressure equalizing (Acibadem; Science ABC)
On descent, rising cabin pressure squeezes the tube shut so it must be actively opened (Acibadem; Science ABC)
Swallowing and yawning contract small soft-palate muscles that pull the tube open (Acibadem; Science ABC)

package.script: Fireflies make cold light. Your old bulb wastes ninety percent as heat, so how do fireflies stay cool? Inside a firefly's tail, sits a glowing organ called the lantern. package.pinned_comment: Before watching, did you think astronauts float because there's no gravity up there? 🚀
package.script: You spin a thousand miles an hour, every day, so why don't you fly off into space? The answer is gravity, and it's weirder than you think. Let's explain it in simple words. Here's the big idea. Everything with mass pulls on everything else. The Earth pulls on you, your phone pulls on your coffee, and you pull on the whole Earth too. Isaac Newton wrote this down in 1687. His rule has two parts. More mass means a stronger pull, and more distance means a weaker one. Double the distance, and the pull drops to just one quarter. The Earth is huge, about six trillion trillion kilograms, so its pull on you wins easily. That pull is what you feel as weight. On the Moon, which has much less mass, you'd weigh about one sixth as much. So, back to the spin. At the equator, you really are moving at about a thousand miles an hour. Spinning does try to fling you outward, like water off a spinning bike wheel. But Earth's gravity is about three hundred times stronger than that fling. So you stay put, held to the ground. For you to float away, Earth would have to spin about seventeen times faster. A whole day would last less than an hour and a half. And you don't feel the spin at all, because the ground, the air and you all move together, smoothly, like passengers on a calm plane. Now here's the wild part. The Moon is falling toward us, right now, and it never stops. Newton pictured a cannon on a mountain. Fire a cannonball slowly, and it curves down and hits the ground. Fire it faster, and it lands farther away. Fire it fast enough, and the ground curves away beneath it as fast as it falls. It keeps falling, and keeps missing. That's an orbit. The Moon does exactly this, falling around the Earth about once every twenty-seven days. The Moon pulls back on us, too. Its gravity tugs on the oceans, making a bulge of water on the side facing the Moon, and another on the far side. As Earth turns through those bulges, most beaches get two high tides a day. And astronauts? On the space station, about two hundred fifty miles up, gravity is still about ninety percent as strong. They float because they're falling, just like that cannonball, racing sideways at seventeen thousand miles an hour. They circle the whole Earth every ninety minutes. Here's the strangest fact of all. Gravity is by far the weakest force in nature. A tiny fridge magnet can lift a paperclip against the pull of the entire planet. Gravity only wins because it adds up, and never switches off. So the next time you jump, remember, you pull the whole Earth up toward you, just a tiny, tiny bit. Next time: what would happen if all the insects disappeared?
key_facts: Earth's equator spins at about 1,000 mph (1,670 km/h)
Gravity at the equator is roughly 300 times stronger than the outward fling of Earth's spin; Earth would need to spin ~17x faster (a day under 1.5 hours) to fling us off
Newton published his law of gravity in 1687 (Principia); pull falls with the square of distance
Earth's mass is about 6 x 10^24 kg; you'd weigh about 1/6 as much on the Moon
The Moon orbits Earth about every 27 days; Newton's cannonball thought experiment explains orbits as falling and missing
The Moon's pull makes two tidal bulges, so most coasts get two high tides a day
The ISS orbits ~250 miles up where gravity is ~90% of surface strength, at ~17,500 mph, one lap every ~90 minutes
Gravity is by far the weakest of the fundamental forces; a small magnet can lift a paperclip against the whole Earth

topic.title: How does a chameleon change colour?

package.title: Chameleons Don't Change Color to Hide 🦎
package.description:
How do chameleons change color? Under their skin, special cells hold a grid of tiny guanine crystals: packed close they reflect blue light (green with the yellow skin on top), and when the chameleon stretches its skin the crystals spread apart and reflect yellow and orange, mostly to signal rivals and mates, not to hide.

package.script: Chameleons don't change color to hide. The real reason is way weirder, and you've probably never heard it: crystals that move thirty percent apart. Under their skin are special cells, packed with tiny crystals, lined up in a neat grid. When a chameleon is calm, the crystals sit close together and bounce back blue light. Add the yellow skin on top, and you get green. But when a rival shows up, the chameleon stretches its skin. The crystals spread farther apart, so now they bounce back yellow and orange. Green turns to fiery orange in just a couple of minutes. It's not hiding, it's showing off. And a deeper layer of crystals reflects the sun's heat, like built-in sunscreen. So if your skin showed your mood, what color would you be right now?
key_facts: Panther chameleons change colour by tuning a lattice of guanine nanocrystals in skin cells called iridophores (Teyssier et al. 2015, Nature Communications; Smithsonian, Mapping Ignorance)

Relaxed: crystals packed close reflect blue, which mixes with the yellow pigment layer above to look green; excited (e.g. a rival male): the lattice spreads out (about 30% less dense) and reflects yellow, orange and red (Mapping Ignorance summary of Teyssier 2015)
Crystal size does not change, only the distance between them; the chameleon changes the spacing by tightening or relaxing its skin (Smithsonian, Mapping Ignorance)
The change can take minutes to fully unfold; script says 'a couple of minutes' (Smithsonian: 'can take minutes')
A deeper skin layer reflects near-infrared light, which likely helps keep the lizard cool in the sun (Smithsonian, hedged in script as 'like built-in sunscreen')
Colour change is mainly for communication and temperature/mood, not camouflage (Smithsonian, Reptiles Magazine)

package.pinned_comment: If your body were a battery, what would you power first? ⚡
package.script: An electric eel can zap you with 600 volts. But how? That's five times your wall outlet, and there's no battery inside. Its body is the battery. Most of that long body is packed with special cells called electrocytes. Each one makes a tiny charge, less than a fifth of a volt. Alone, that's nothing. But they're stacked in rows, thousands of them, head to tail, like batteries in a flashlight. When the eel spots a fish, its brain fires one signal, and every cell flips on at once. About six thousand tiny charges add up to one giant shock. Zap! The fish freezes on the spot. Here's the twist: an electric eel isn't even an eel. It's a knifefish, closer to a catfish. So if your body were a battery, what would you power first?
key_facts: The shock comes from the Main and Hunter's organs: some 5,000 to 6,000 stacked electroplaques (electrocytes), working like a battery (Fluke); script says 'about six thousand'
Each electrocyte makes only about 0.15 volt (Fluke); script says 'less than a fifth of a volt', screen shows 0.15 V
A motor-neuron signal opens ion channels so each cell becomes a dipole, and many cells firing together add up to a strong shock (Science ABC)
Electric eels reach about 600 volts (Fluke: up to 500 V; record before 2019 was 650 V; E. voltai measured 860 V, FAPESP); US wall outlet is 120 V, so 600 V = 5x
The electric organ fills most of the body (about two-thirds per Science ABC; script says 'most of that long body')
Electric eels are not true eels: they are knifefishes, more closely related to catfish and carp (FAPESP, Science ABC)

package.pinned_comment: Claws, hairs or the non-stick coating: which spider trick would you steal? 🕷️
package.hook_text: Spider glue almost never lets a fly go. So why do you never see the spider stuck?
package.script: Spider glue almost never lets a fly go. So why do you never see the spider stuck? Secret one: most of the web isn't sticky. The spokes are dry silk. Only the spiral has beads of glue, so the spider walks the spokes. Secret two: its feet. Web spiders have three claws per foot. Insects get two. The extra claw hooks a single thread, like a tiny hand. But here's the wild part. Building one web, a spider touches its own glue hundreds of times. Its legs are covered in branched hairs, so the glue slides along them and drips off. Scientists washed spider legs, and they stuck more. So there's a non-stick coating, too. A fly hits lots of glue at once. The spider barely touches a drop. So which trick would you steal: the claws, the hairs, or the coating?
key_facts: Orb webs: the radial spokes are dry silk, only the spiral carries glue droplets (How It Works; Burke Museum: webs have many non-sticky threads)
Web-building spiders have a third tarsal claw that grips single threads; insects have at most two (Burke Museum)

Branched hairs on the legs let glue droplets slide along and drip off; washing legs with hexane made them stick more, showing a non-stick coating (Smithsonian / phys.org)
Spiders tiptoe around the glue and touch few droplets, while a fly hits many at once (Burke Museum, Vollrath & Tillinghast 1992)

package.title: What If 10 Quintillion Insects Vanished Tonight? 🐝
package.description:
What would happen if all the insects on Earth disappeared? We walk through it step by step: pollination and the fruits we'd lose (including chocolate), hungry songbirds and fish, Australia's cow-pat problem and the dung beetles that fixed it, and whether humans would starve.

package.pinned_comment: Which food would you miss most if insects vanished: chocolate, apples or honey?
package.script: Every insect on Earth vanishes tonight. What would you lose first? The first thing you'd notice is the quiet, no buzzing, no chirping, no crickets at night. But the real trouble starts sooner than you think. Let's walk through it, step by step. First, how many bugs are we talking about? Scientists think about ten quintillion insects are alive right now. That's more than a billion insects for every single person. Over a million kinds have names, and millions more are still waiting for one. So when they all disappear, they leave a gigantic hole. Start with the flowers. Nearly nine out of ten flowering plants need animals to carry their pollen, and most of those animals are insects. Bees, flies, beetles, moths and butterflies move pollen from flower to flower, so the plant can make seeds and fruit. Without them, the flowers still bloom, but most never turn into fruit. About three quarters of our main food crops get help from pollinators. Apples, almonds, blueberries, cherries and melons would become rare and very expensive. And chocolate? Cacao flowers are pollinated by tiny flies called midges, about the size of a pinhead. No midges, almost no chocolate. Next come the animals that eat insects. Most songbirds feed their chicks on bugs, even the ones that eat seeds as adults. One pair of chickadees needs six to nine thousand caterpillars to raise a single nest of chicks. Bats, frogs, lizards and spiders lose their dinner too. In rivers, trout and many other fish eat young mayflies and caddisflies. Take away the bugs, and the food chain crumbles from the bottom up. Now for the gross part. Insects are nature's cleanup crew. Beetles and fly larvae break down dead leaves, dead animals, and poop. Australia found this out the hard way. When settlers brought cattle, the local dung beetles couldn't handle cow pats. The pats sat in the fields for months, smothering the grass and breeding swarms of flies. So scientists shipped in dung beetles from abroad, and about twenty-three kinds settled in. Now picture that problem everywhere on Earth. Fungi and bacteria would keep working, but much more slowly. So, would humans starve? Not right away. Wheat, rice and corn are pollinated by the wind, so we'd still have bread, rice and popcorn. But our plates would get very boring, and we'd lose honey, silk, and lots of fruits and vegetables. Many wild plants would slowly fade away, and the animals that eat them would follow. Even the soil would suffer, because insects dig it, mix it and feed it. So the next time a bee buzzes past your head, remember, that tiny bug helps keep your whole plate full. Next time: how a bear hunt gave us the teddy bear.

package.title: Why Do Onions Make You Cry After 30 Seconds? 🧅
package.description:
Why do onions make you cry? Cutting an onion mixes a sulfur compound with an enzyme, and a second enzyme (found in 2002) turns the result into syn-propanethial-S-oxide, an irritating gas that peaks about 30 seconds after the cut and makes your tear glands wash it away.

package.pinned_comment: Would you still eat a plant that fights back with tear gas? 🧅 Yes or no?
package.script: Onions fire tear gas at your eyes, 30 seconds after you cut them. How? Inside every onion cell, two chemicals are kept apart, in separate little rooms. One is a sulfur molecule. The other is an enzyme. Your knife smashes the walls, and they finally mix. The enzyme turns the sulfur into an acid, then a second enzyme, only discovered in 2002, flips that acid into a gas. It drifts up, and peaks about 30 seconds after the cut. When it hits your eyes, tiny nerves shout "burning!" So your tear glands flood your eyes, to wash it away. Why bother? It's armor. Any animal that bites an onion, gets a face full of sting. Want fewer tears? Cut it under running water. So, would you still eat a plant that fights back with tear gas?

Alliinase turns the sulfoxides into sulfenic acids

The tear-causing compound peaks about 30 seconds after the onion is cut
Corneal nerve endings sense it as burning and tear glands wash it away

package.title: Why Honey Starts As 80% Water 🐝
package.description:
How do bees make honey? Bees sip flower nectar (up to 80% water) into their honey stomach, add enzymes that split the sugar, pass it mouth to mouth in the hive, then fan it with their wings until it's about 18% water and seal it with wax.

package.pinned_comment: So which is it: is honey flower juice, or bee spit? 🐝 Tell me your answer!
package.script: Your honey was once 80 percent water, and you'd never guess how bees dried it. It starts with nectar, sugary flower juice. A bee sips it into a second stomach, called the honey stomach. Enzymes from her spit, start chopping the sugar into smaller sugars. Back at the hive, she spits it mouth to mouth, to a house bee, who chews on it for up to 20 minutes. Then it goes into a wax cell. But it's still way too runny. So the bees fan it with their wings, blowing the water away, until it's only about 18 percent water. That's so thick, germs can't grow in it. Then they cap each cell, with wax. One bee makes just a twelfth of a teaspoon, in her whole life. So, is your honey flower juice, or bee spit?
key_facts: Nectar is about 70-80% water (MSU Extension; EarthDate)
Foragers store nectar in the honey stomach (crop) and add invertase, which splits sucrose into glucose and fructose (MSU Extension)
House bees pass nectar back and forth for up to ~20 minutes, then store it in cells (EarthDate)
Bees fan with their wings until honey is ~18% water, too concentrated for microbes; cells are capped with wax (MSU Extension; EarthDate)
A worker bee makes about 1/12 teaspoon of honey in her lifetime (commonly cited; PBS NOVA via Local Hive)

A shrimp smaller than your finger,
fires a bubble almost as hot as the Sun.

key_facts: The pistol shrimp's big claw has a plug that slams into a socket when it snaps shut, firing a water jet (about 90 km/h, ~25 m/s)

The bubble collapses in well under a millisecond and its inside is estimated to reach about 4,700°C (over 5,000 K), close to the Sun's surface (~5,500°C)
The collapse emits a brief flash of light (shrimpoluminescence, Lohse et al., Nature 2001)
The snap's sound comes from the bubble collapse, not the claw closing; it is among the loudest sounds in the ocean and can stun small prey

package.script: In nineteen-oh-two, a president refused to shoot one bear, and that's why your teddy bear exists. Here's how it all started, on a muddy hunting trip in Mississippi. It's November. President Theodore Roosevelt is out in the swamps, on a bear hunt with the state's governor. After days of searching, Roosevelt hasn't seen a single bear. So his guide, Holt Collier, tracks one down with the hunting dogs, and ties it to a tree. Everyone waits for the president to shoot. But Roosevelt says no. Shooting a tied-up bear isn't fair, so he refuses. A few days later, a cartoonist named Clifford Berryman draws the moment for the Washington Post. In his cartoon, the bear is small and scared, with big round eyes. Readers love it. Berryman keeps drawing that little bear for years, like Roosevelt's furry sidekick. Now jump to Brooklyn, New York. Morris and Rose Michtom run a small shop, selling candy and toys. They see the cartoon, and Rose sews a soft, stuffed bear. They put it in the window, with a sign that says, Teddy's bear. The story goes, they even wrote to Roosevelt to ask if they could use his name. The bears sell out fast. So many people want one, the Michtoms start a whole toy company, called Ideal. But here's the twist. At almost the same time, in Germany, a toy maker called Steiff was making bears too. Margarete Steiff started the company by sewing felt elephants. Her nephew Richard loved sketching bears, and he designed one with arms and legs that move. In nineteen-oh-three, he took it to a big toy fair in Leipzig. At first, almost nobody cared. Then an American buyer ordered three thousand. By nineteen-oh-seven, Steiff was making nine hundred seventy-four thousand bears. So the teddy bear was born twice, on two continents, at almost the same moment. Now look closely at a teddy from back then. Long snout, low forehead, skinny arms. It looks like a real bear. topic.title: Why don't hippos get sunburned?

package.title: Why Don't Hippos Get Sunburned? 🦛
package.description:
Why don't hippos get sunburned? Glands under a hippo's skin ooze a clear fluid that turns red, then orange-brown, within minutes; its red and orange pigments (hipposudoric and norhipposudoric acid) soak up UV light like a natural sunscreen, and the red one also stopped bacteria growing in lab tests.

package.script: Hippos sweat red goo, and you'll never see one sunburned. But why? A hippo spends hours in the African sun, with almost no hair to protect it. So its skin fights back. Glands under the skin ooze a thick, clear goo. Within a few minutes, it turns bright red, then a rusty orange-brown. That's why people call it blood sweat. But it's not blood, and it's not really sweat. The color comes from two pigments, one red, one orange. Together, they soak up ultraviolet light, like built-in sunscreen. And the red one does even more. In lab tests, it stopped nasty bacteria from growing. Handy, when rivals leave scratches all over you. So a hippo makes its own sunscreen, and its own antibiotic. If you could sweat any color, which one would you pick?

The secretion absorbs UV and visible light (200-600 nm), acting as a sunscreen (JEB; Nature News)
In lab tests the red pigment inhibited Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae (Nature News); hippos are often scarred from fights, which can get infected (Nature News)

topic.title: How do penguins keep their feet from freezing?

package.title: Penguins Keep Their Feet at 0°C On Purpose 🐧
package.description:
How do penguins keep their feet from freezing on the ice? Warm blood flowing down their legs runs right beside cold blood coming back up, so heat is swapped before it reaches the feet (countercurrent heat exchange), and the feet stay just above freezing while rocking back on their heels and tail keeps the toes off the ice.

package.pinned_comment: How long do you think YOUR bare toes would last on Antarctic ice? 🧊
package.script:
You'd lose your toes on this ice.
Emperor penguins stand on it for two months.
The secret is in their legs.
Warm blood flowing down to the feet
runs right beside cold blood coming back up.
So the heat jumps across,
like passing a hot potato.
By the time blood reaches the toes,
it's just above freezing.
Cold toes lose very little heat to the ice,
and the warmth goes back into the body.
Feet near zero degrees,
body near thirty-eight.
If the toes get too cold,
the penguin widens its arteries,
and sends down a little more warm blood.
Still chilly?
It rocks back on its heels and stiff tail,
lifting its toes off the ice,
and hunches down,
so belly feathers blanket its feet.
A penguin keeps its feet cold on purpose.
So how long would your toes last out there?

topic.title: Why are you taller in the morning than at night?

package.title: Why You're 1 cm Taller Every Morning 📏
package.description:
Why are you taller in the morning than at night? All day, gravity squeezes water out of the 23 squishy discs in your spine so you shrink about a centimeter by bedtime, and while you sleep the discs soak water back up like sponges.

package.pinned_comment: Measure yourself tonight and tomorrow morning: how much taller were you? 📏
package.script: You lose one centimeter of height every day, but why? Your spine isn't one solid bone. It's a stack of vertebrae, with twenty-three squishy discs in between. Each disc is like a jelly doughnut, with a soft, watery middle. All day, gravity pushes down on you. Every step and every sit squeezes a little water out, and the discs flatten a tiny bit. Add up all twenty-three, and you've shrunk about a centimeter by bedtime. But when you lie down to sleep, the weight comes off your spine. The discs soak water back up, like little sponges, and by morning, you're tall again. In space, with no gravity, astronauts can grow three percent taller! So tonight, measure yourself before bed, then again when you wake up. Will you be one centimeter taller tomorrow morning?
key_facts: The intervertebral discs between vertebrae compress under load during the day, so people are typically around 1 cm (often quoted up to about 2 cm) shorter by evening (scienceblog; mechse.illinois.edu)
The adult spine has 23 intervertebral discs, each with a tough outer ring (annulus fibrosus) and a soft, water-rich gel centre (nucleus pulposus)
Lying down removes the load and the discs rehydrate overnight, restoring height by morning
Without gravity, astronauts' spines lengthen and they can grow up to about 3% taller in space (Scientific American; Space.com)

package.title: How Do Animals Survive 7 Months Frozen Solid?
package.description:
How do animals survive being frozen solid? Wood frogs freeze with no heartbeat for months, Arctic ground squirrels supercool below zero, Antarctic fish make antifreeze proteins, and tardigrades dry out and wake up decades later.

package.pinned_comment: Which trick would you pick to survive the winter: sugar, supercooling, antifreeze, or drying out?
package.script: Frozen solid for seven months. No heartbeat. No breathing. You'd be dead. This frog just hops away in spring. So how do animals survive being frozen? Today, four champions of the cold, each with a totally different trick. Meet the wood frog. It lives as far north as Alaska, and it doesn't hide from winter. It just lies down under the leaves, and lets the ice come. The problem with freezing is sharp ice crystals. If they grow inside a cell, they rip it apart like tiny knives. So the frog plays a clever game. As ice touches its skin, its liver floods the body with sugar, up to ten times the normal amount. That sugar soaks into every cell, like a syrup that won't freeze. So the ice can only grow outside the cells, in the spaces in between. Up to sixty percent of the frog turns to ice. No heartbeat. No breath. In Alaska, it can stay like this for as long as seven months. Then spring comes, the ice melts, and the heart starts beating again. Our second champion uses the opposite trick. The Arctic ground squirrel never freezes at all, even when its body drops below zero. Scientists measured one at almost minus three degrees, the coldest body ever found in a mammal. How? It's called supercooling. Water needs a tiny seed to start freezing, like a speck of dust, or a bit of ice. The squirrel's blood is so clean, there's nothing for ice to grow on. So it stays liquid, below freezing. But that's risky. So every few weeks, the squirrel shivers, warms itself back up for a little while, then drops back into the deep cold. Now, dive under the Antarctic ice. The sea here is almost minus two degrees, cold enough to freeze most fish solid. But these Antarctic fish swim around just fine. Their blood is full of antifreeze proteins. When a tiny ice crystal sneaks in, the proteins grab onto it, and wrap it up so it can't grow. One of their cousins, the icefish, went even further. Its blood has no red cells at all. It's clear, like water. And then there's the toughest of them all. The tardigrade, or water bear, smaller than a grain of sand. When things get bad, it dries itself out, curls into a tiny ball called a tun, and basically pauses its life. In nineteen eighty three, scientists collected moss in Antarctica, and kept it in a freezer at minus twenty. Thirty years later, they thawed it out. Two water bears woke up, and one of them went on to lay nineteen eggs. So why do scientists care? Because we can't do this yet. A donor heart on ice only lasts about four to six hours. Researchers are studying the frog's sugar, and the fish's antifreeze, to keep organs alive for much longer. Four animals, four tricks: sugar, supercooling, antifreeze, and drying out. Which one would you pick? Next time, how did a bitter bean become the world's favorite treat, chocolate?
key_facts: Wood frogs: up to ~60% of the body freezes, heart and breathing stop, glucose up to ~10x normal acts as a cryoprotectant; in Alaska up to ~7 months frozen (Audubon)
Arctic ground squirrel: supercools to about -2.9 C, lowest body temperature recorded in a mammal; rewarms every few weeks (UAF)
Antarctic notothenioid fish: seawater about -1.9 C, antifreeze glycoproteins bind ice crystals; icefish have no red blood cells / hemoglobin, colorless blood (Wikipedia: Antarctic fishes)
Tardigrades: moss collected in Antarctica Nov 1983, stored at -20 C, thawed 2014; two revived, one laid 19 eggs (phys.org 2016)
Donor hearts are typically kept on ice for about 4-6 hours

package.title: Why Can't You Tickle Yourself? 0.2 Seconds Changes It 🤔
package.description:
Why can't you tickle yourself? Your cerebellum predicts the touch from your own movement and turns the feeling down, but in a robot experiment, adding a delay of just 0.2 seconds made self-tickling feel more ticklish.

Sources:
https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/why-cant-a-person-tickle/
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1038/2870
https://www.sciencealert.com/the-scientific-reason-you-can-t-tickle-yourself

package.pinned_comment: Have you EVER managed to tickle yourself? Tell me how 👇
package.script: Your brain cancels your own tickles before you feel them. But how? Every time you move, your brain sends a copy of the order to the cerebellum, at the back of your head. It predicts what the touch will feel like, then turns the feeling down. No surprise, no tickle. When someone else tickles you, there's no prediction. Your brain can't guess where or when, so it hits full blast. Scientists tested this with a robot. People moved a handle, and a robot brushed their palm. Moving it themselves? Barely ticklish. Then the robot added a delay of just two tenths of a second. Suddenly, it felt more ticklish. The prediction was off, so the brain couldn't cancel it. So your own brain blocks the tickle. Can you find a way to outsmart it?
key_facts: Every movement sends a copy of the motor command to the cerebellum, which predicts the sensory result and dampens it (Blakemore, Wolpert & Frith).
Touch from someone else can't be predicted, so it isn't dampened.
In a robot-arm experiment, delaying the self-produced touch by 0.2 seconds made it feel more ticklish.

package.description:
Why do sharks never run out of teeth? Shark teeth sit in soft tissue instead of bone, and rows of spare teeth folded inside the jaw roll forward like a conveyor belt whenever one falls out.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shark_tooth
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/videos/a-great-white-can-go-through-20000-teeth-in-i/

package.script:
This shark will lose thirty thousand teeth.
So why does it never run out?
Look inside its jaw.
Behind the front teeth,
there are rows and rows of spares,
folded back against the inside of the jaw.
Most sharks carry about fifteen rows.
Your teeth are locked into bone.
A shark's teeth sit in soft tissue,
so they pop out easily.
When one snaps off,
the tooth behind it swings up,
and takes its place,
sometimes in just one day.
Meanwhile, a brand new tooth
starts growing at the very back.
It's like a moving staircase of teeth,
always rolling forward.
A great white goes through
about twenty thousand teeth in its life.
And this lemon shark?
Scientists think more than thirty thousand.
So how many teeth have you lost so far?
key_facts: Shark teeth are held by connective (soft) tissue, not set into bone, so they come out easily (Save Our Seas; Wikipedia)
Rows of replacement teeth lie folded back against the inside of the jaw and move up when a front tooth is lost (Save Our Seas)
Most sharks have about 15 rows of teeth in each jaw (Wikipedia)
A lost tooth can be replaced in as little as a day / 24 hours (Wikipedia; Save Our Seas)
A great white can grow up to 20,000 teeth in a lifetime (Smithsonian)
A lemon shark may shed more than 30,000 teeth over its lifespan (Save Our Seas, calculation)
